tool: CDC STEADI Stay Independent: Check Your Risk for Falling
attribution: Developed by the Greater Los Angeles VA Geriatric Research Education Clinical Center and affiliates; validated fall risk self-assessment (Rubenstein et al. J Safety Res; 2011: 42(6)493-499).
scoring: Add the points for each Yes answer. No answers score 0.

at_risk_rule.description: At risk if total >= 4, or if total < 4 but the person fell in the past year.

questions.text: I have fallen in the past year.
questions.why: People who have fallen once are likely to fall again.

questions.text: I use or have been advised to use a cane or walker to get around safely.
questions.why: People who have been advised to use a cane or walker may already be more likely to fall.

questions.text: Sometimes I feel unsteady when I am walking.
questions.why: Unsteadiness or needing support while walking are signs of poor balance.

questions.text: I steady myself by holding onto furniture when walking at home.
questions.why: This is also a sign of poor balance.
People who are worried about falling are more likely to fall.

questions.text: I need to push with my hands to stand up from a chair.
questions.why: This is a sign of weak leg muscles, a major reason for falling.

questions.text: I have some trouble stepping up onto a curb.
questions.why: This is also a sign of weak leg muscles.

questions.text: I often have to rush to the toilet.
questions.why: Rushing to the bathroom, especially at night, increases your chance of falling.

questions.text: I have lost some feeling in my feet.
questions.why: Numbness in your feet can cause stumbles and lead to falls.

questions.text: I take medicine that sometimes makes me feel light-headed or more tired than usual.
questions.why: Side effects from medicines can sometimes increase your chance of falling.

questions.text: I take medicine to help me sleep or improve my mood.
questions.why: These medicines can sometimes increase your chance of falling.

questions.text: I often feel sad or depressed.
questions.why: Symptoms of depression, such as not feeling well or feeling slowed down, are linked to falls.
